The dataset comprises 20,058 games collected from Lichess.org, of which 80.5% are rated. The remaining 19.5% are casual (unrated) games. Games end through four primary mechanisms: resignation (55.6%), checkmate (31.5%), timeout (8.4%), and draws (4.7%).

Figure 1: Winner distribution (left) and game end method (right) across all 20,058 games.
Figure 2: Outcome distribution comparing rated versus unrated games. Rated games show slightly more decisive outcomes and fewer draws.
Key Observation: White wins 52.3% of decisive games — a clear first-move advantage. Resignation is the most common game-ending method (55.6%), indicating that players typically recognize lost positions rather than playing to mate. Checkmates account for 31.5% of all games.
Section 2

White vs. Black: The First-Move Advantage

Statistical Significance (Binomial Test)

Across all 19,108 decisive games, white wins 52.3% and black wins 47.7% — a difference of 4.7 percentage points. This advantage is statistically significant (two-sided binomial test, p < 0.001), confirming that white's first-move initiative translates to a real and measurable winning edge on Lichess.

Figure 3: Overall win rates for white and black in decisive games. The dashed line represents 50% (no advantage).
Figure 4: White and black win rates broken down by how the game ended. Note how timeout games show the most balanced distribution.
Figure 5: Win rates by rating bracket. White's advantage persists across all skill levels, with some variation in magnitude.
Figure 6: Win rates by time control category. Faster time controls may slightly alter the white advantage dynamic.

Higher-Rated Wins (|diff| > 200)

Player ratings span a wide range typical of online chess. The average white rating is 1597 (median 1567) and average black rating is 1589 (median 1562). The distributions are nearly identical, confirming no systematic rating-based color assignment bias.

Figure 7: Distribution of white and black player ratings. Both distributions mirror each other closely, centered around ~1500.
Figure 8: White win probability as a function of the rating differential (white_rating minus black_rating). The relationship is strongly monotonic — each ~100-point rating advantage translates to a measurable increase in expected win rate. Game counts shown at the bottom of each bar.

The Pearson correlation between rating differential and white win probability is r = 0.367, indicating a strong linear relationship. When the rating gap exceeds 200 points (in either direction), the higher-rated player wins 64.6% of decisive games — demonstrating that skill, as measured by Elo rating, is the dominant predictor of game outcomes.

Figure 9: Average game length (in turns) by rating bracket. Higher-rated players consistently play longer games — a reflection of deeper opening knowledge, superior defensive technique, and fewer early blunders.

Opening Depth Analysis

The average opening phase lasts 4.8 plies (half-moves), ranging from 1 to 28. Longer opening phases correlate with higher-rated games — stronger players tend to know deeper theory. The relationship between opening depth and outcome is subtle: games where white wins have an average opening ply of 4.9, black wins average 4.7, and draws average 5.1.

Section 6

Key Findings and Strategic Takeaways

♟ White holds a measurable, consistent first-move advantage

Across all decisive games, white wins 52.3% compared to black's 47.7% — a 4.7 percentage-point edge. This advantage is statistically significant (binomial test p < 1.04e-10). The effect persists across all rating brackets and time controls, though it varies in magnitude.

📊 Rating differential is the strongest predictor of outcome

The Pearson correlation between rating differential and white win probability is r = 0.367. When the rating gap exceeds 200 points in either direction, the higher-rated player wins 64.6% of decisive games. The relationship is monotonic: every ~100-point rating advantage translates to an additional ~6-8 percentage points in win probability.

📖 Opening choice matters — 365 distinct ECO codes observed

The most popular opening is "Van't Kruijs Opening" (368 games, white wins 35.8%). 6 openings in the top 15 show better outcomes for black, with the most black-favorable being "Van't Kruijs Opening" (black wins 64.2% vs white 35.8%). Openings with higher black win rates tend to be those where white overextends or black has well-established equalizing lines.

⏱ Faster time controls dramatically increase timeout frequency

In Bullet/UltraBullet games (≤3 min), 12.8% of games end by timeout, compared to just 4.3% in Classical (30+ min). Conversely, checkmate is far more common in slower formats. Average game length increases from ~48 turns in Bullet to ~50 turns in Classical — faster games favor speed and flagging over positional depth.

📈 Higher-rated players play longer, more complex games

Games in the highest rating bracket (2300+) average 74 turns, compared to 52 turns in the lowest bracket (<1100). Higher-rated games also see a higher proportion of checkmates and fewer early resignations, suggesting deeper tactical resilience at higher skill levels.

🤝 Draw rate is 4.7% overall but varies sharply by rating

While only 4.7% of all games end in a draw, this rate climbs significantly with rating — players above 2000 draw at approximately 2-3× the rate of players below 1400. This reflects the increased difficulty of converting advantages against stronger defensive play.

Strategic Takeaways for Players:
1. Leverage the white pieces. With a 4.7 pp advantage, playing as white is a measurable edge. Prepare aggressive opening repertoires that maximize the initiative.
2. Target rating mismatches. Rating differential is the single strongest predictor — a 200-point gap yields a ~65% win rate for the stronger player.
3. Choose openings strategically. While most openings favor white, 6 of the top 15 give black better results. Study these lines for your black repertoire.
4. Adapt to the clock. In bullet/blitz, flagging awareness matters as much as chess knowledge. In classical, invest time in the middlegame — the extra depth pays off.
5. Higher-rated games are longer. Build endurance and deep calculation ability to compete at higher rating levels where games routinely exceed 80 turns.
